ticket_data.title: StepValueValidator accepts invalid values and crashes on large numbers
ticket_data.description:
`StepValueValidator` uses `math.remainder()`. That converts values to float. Large integers and Decimals lose precision or crash.

{{{#!python
from decimal import Decimal
from django import forms

forms.IntegerField(step_size=2).clean("9007199254740993")
# Returns 9007199254740993. It is odd, so it should be rejected.

forms.IntegerField(step_size=2).clean("9" * 400)
# OverflowError: int too large to convert to float

forms.DecimalField(step_size=Decimal("0.1")).clean("1e400")
# ValueError: math domain error

forms.DecimalField(step_size=Decimal("0.01")).clean("12345678901234567.01")
# ValidationError, but the value is a valid multiple of 0.01
}}}

The first case lets an invalid value through. The next two raise an unhandled exception, so user input can cause a 500 error.

Floats are also used for the tolerance (`abs_tol=1e-9`). So `Decimal("1.00000000005")` is accepted with a step of `Decimal("1e-10")`.

I think int and Decimal values should be checked with exact arithmetic. The float path can stay as it is. Be careful not to turn the Decimal into a huge number: `Fraction(Decimal("1e50000000"))` takes about a minute.

I am happy to work on a patch once this is accepted.

ticket_data.title: Drop support for Python 3.12 & 3.13
ticket_data.description:
Django 6.2 LTS, supported until April 2030, is the last version to support:
- Python 3.12 (end of life: October 2028)
- Python 3.13 (end of life: October 2029)

Per [https://github.com/django/deps/blob/main/accepted/0020-annual-release-cycle.rst DEP 20], each feature release supports the two Python versions receiving bug fixes at the start of its pre-release phase, plus the most recent one to have moved to security fixes only. Django 2028 therefore supports Python 3.14, 3.15, and 3.16.

See [https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/dev/faq/install/#what-python-version-can-i-use-with-django our policy about Python version support]. For Django 2028, the dates work out like this:

- Django 2028 is released in January 2028 and reaches end of life in December 2030.
- Python 3.14, its oldest supported Python, was released in October 2025 and gets five years of upstream support, so it reaches end of life in October 2030.

The same holds every year: Django 2029 supports 3.15 through 3.17, and 3.15 reaches end of life in October 2031, two months before 2029 does in December 2031.

ticket_data.title: order_by("pk") on a union() of a composite pk model crashes or sorts wrongly
ticket_data.description:
{{{#!python
class Comment(models.Model):
    pk = models.CompositePrimaryKey("tenant_id", "comment_id")
    tenant_id = models.IntegerField()
    comment_id = models.IntegerField()

# rows (tenant_id, comment_id): (1, 2), (2, 1), (1, 1)
qs = Comment.objects.filter(tenant_id=1).union(Comment.objects.filter(tenant_id=2))
}}}

Ordering a combined query by a composite primary key fails in two ways.

1. On a normal queryset, `order_by("pk")` crashes. `first()` crashes too, because it orders by `pk`.

{{{#!python
qs.first()
qs.order_by("pk")  # when evaluated
# TypeError: 'NoneType' object does not support item assignment
}}}

The error is raised in `Query.add_select_col()` (called from `SQLCompiler.get_order_by()`), because `query.selected` is `None`.

2. With `values_list("pk")` there is no error, but the order is wrong.

{{{#!python
list(qs.values_list("pk").order_by("pk"))
# [((1, 1),), ((2, 1),), ((1, 2),)]
# expected: [((1, 1),), ((1, 2),), ((2, 1),)]
}}}

The SQL ends with `ORDER BY "col1"`, and `col1` is only the last pk column (`comment_id`). The same query without `union()` is ordered correctly.

I think `get_order_by()` treats the composite pk (`ColPairs`) as a single column in the combinator branch. It should order by each column of the pk.

Related: #36065, #37354 (other composite pk ordering bugs).

ticket_data.title: Lexemes with only escaped characters cause a crash
ticket_data.description:
Searching for `Lexeme('&')` passes the provided value through `psql_escape`, which returns `None`. When UTF8Dumper calls `bytes(None, "utf-8")`:
{{{
ERROR: test_quote_lexeme (postgres_tests.test_search.TestLexemes.test_quote_lexeme) (lexeme='&')
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/pdi/dev/django/tests/postgres_tests/test_search.py", line 886, in test_quote_lexeme
    self.assertEqual(quote_lexeme(lexeme), quoted)
                     ~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^
  File "/home/pdi/dev/django/django/contrib/postgres/search.py", line 26, in quote_lexeme
    return UTF8Dumper(str).quote(psql_escape(value)).decode()
           ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/home/pdi/dev/django/.venv/lib/python3.14/site-packages/psycopg/adapt.py", line 59, in quote
    if (value := self.dump(obj)) is None:
                 ~~~~~~~~~^^^^^
  File "/home/pdi/dev/django/django/contrib/postgres/search.py", line 23, in dump
    return bytes(obj, "utf-8")
TypeError: encoding without a string argument
}}}

See the attached patch to reproduce in the django test suite.

Lexeme is documented as:
> Lexeme objects allow search operators to be safely used with strings from an untrusted source. The content of each lexeme is escaped so that any operators that may exist in the string itself will not be interpreted.

ticket_data.title: No system check for GenericRelation on a model with DB_CASCADE, leaving orphaned generic rows
ticket_data.description:
The docs say that database-level and Python-level `on_delete` variants cannot be mixed in the same model or in related models. System checks enforce this with `models.E050` and `fields.E323`.

`GenericRelation` is a Python-level cleanup, but it is not checked. If a model has a `GenericRelation` and a `DB_CASCADE` foreign key, the database deletes the model's rows and Django never deletes the generic related objects. They stay in the table with no error and no check warning.

{{{#!python
class Tag(models.Model):
    content_type = models.ForeignKey(ContentType, models.CASCADE)
    object_id = models.PositiveIntegerField()
    content_object = GenericForeignKey()


class Author(models.Model):
    pass


class Book(models.Model):
    author = models.ForeignKey(Author, models.DB_CASCADE)
    tags = GenericRelation(Tag)
}}}

{{{#!python
>>> author = Author.objects.create()
>>> book = Book.objects.create(author=author)
>>> book.tags.create()
>>> author.delete()
>>> Book.objects.count(), Tag.objects.count()
(0, 1)
}}}

`manage.py check` reports no issues. With `models.CASCADE` instead of `models.DB_CASCADE`, the `Tag` row is deleted.

Why it happens: `Collector.collect()` skips `DB_CASCADE` relations, so `Book` instances are never collected. Their private fields are never visited, so `GenericRelation.bulk_related_objects()` never runs. `GenericRelation.remote_field.on_delete` is `DO_NOTHING`, so `Model._check_related_fields()` does not see it as a Python-level variant.

I verified this on 6.1.3 and on main with SQLite. I also ran random schemas with database and Python `on_delete` variants against the equivalent all-Python schemas. Among schemas that pass all checks, the only difference in the final data was orphaned generic rows.

Suggested fix: add a system check error for a model that has a `GenericRelation` (any private field with `bulk_related_objects()`) and a `DB_CASCADE` foreign key. It would not fire for `DB_SET_NULL` or `DB_SET_DEFAULT`, because those do not delete the model's rows. This is the same kind of gap as #37254 (implicit M2M through tables), which was fixed in 6.1.x.

I am happy to work on a patch once the approach is agreed.

ticket_data.title: Tutorial part 4, explicit list for reverse() args
ticket_data.description:
The current version (https://github.com/django/django/blob/main/docs/intro/tutorial04.txt#L106) is creating an implicit list by using a trailing comma. I suggest to use an explicit list instead to both be inline with the documentation and avoid user error/confusion.

I already have a pull request to address this issue (https://github.com/django/django/pull/22246).

ticket_data.title: Database session backends crash on session keys containing a null character
ticket_data.description:
A request with the header {{{Cookie: sessionid="AAAAAAAA\000"}}} (printable ASCII only) returns HTTP 500 when using the {{{db}}} or {{{cached_db}}} session backend on PostgreSQL.

{{{http.cookies}}} unquotes the {{{\000}}} escape into a null character. {{{SessionBase._validate_session_key()}}} accepts the key, because it checks only {{{key and len(key) >= 8}}}. {{{SessionStore._get_session_from_db()}}} (and {{{_aget_session_from_db()}}}) then passes it to the database. PostgreSQL's driver rejects it (psycopg 3 raises {{{DataError}}}, psycopg2 raises {{{ValueError}}}), and the exception propagates out of {{{SessionMiddleware}}}. Because the session loads in middleware, every URL is affected, and the 500 response doesn't clear the cookie, so a client holding it keeps getting 500s until the cookie is removed.

The {{{cache}}}, {{{file}}} and {{{signed_cookies}}} backends, and the {{{db}}} backend on SQLite, return 200 for the same cookie.

To reproduce, save the script below as {{{poc.py}}}, then run these commands in the same directory. They need Docker and Python 3.12 or later; the container is removed on stop.

{{{#!sh
python3 -m venv djnul-venv
. djnul-venv/bin/activate
docker run --rm -d --name djnul -e POSTGRES_DB=djnul -e POSTGRES_HOST_AUTH_METHOD=trust -p 55432:5432 postgres:17
until docker exec djnul pg_isready -h localhost -U postgres -q; do sleep 1; done
pip install "Django>=6.0,<6.1" "psycopg[binary]"
PGHOST=localhost PGPORT=55432 PGUSER=postgres python poc.py
docker stop djnul
}}}

It prints {{{crafted: 500}}} and {{{normal: 200}}}. To test main instead, install {{{git+https://github.com/django/django.git}}} in place of the Django release. The script sets only the database {{{NAME}}}, so psycopg picks up the host, port and user from the {{{PG*}}} environment variables.

{{{#!python
import django
from django.conf import settings

settings.configure(
    DEBUG=False,
    ALLOWED_HOSTS=["testserver"],
    SECRET_KEY="x",
    DATABASES={"default": {"ENGINE": "django.db.backends.postgresql", "NAME": "djnul"}},
    INSTALLED_APPS=["django.contrib.contenttypes", "django.contrib.auth", "django.contrib.sessions"],
    MIDDLEWARE=["django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware"],
    ROOT_URLCONF="__main__",
)
django.setup()

from django.core.management import call_command
from django.http import HttpResponse
from django.test import Client
from django.urls import path

def view(request):
    request.session.get("x")
    return HttpResponse("ok")

urlpatterns = [path("", view)]

call_command("migrate", run_syncdb=True, verbosity=0)
client = Client(raise_request_exception=False)
print("crafted:", client.get("/", HTTP_COOKIE='sessionid="AAAAAAAA\\000"').status_code)  # 500
print("normal: ", client.get("/", HTTP_COOKIE="sessionid=" + "a" * 32).status_code)  # 200
}}}

Tested on Django 6.0.9 and main, with psycopg 3 and psycopg2. The code is the same on 5.2, 6.0, 6.1 and main.

Proposed fix: make {{{_validate_session_key()}}} also reject keys containing a null character, so such a key becomes "no session", the same as an unknown key. Restricting keys to {{{VALID_KEY_CHARS}}} (as the file backend does) would be stricter, but it would break the {{{signed_cookies}}} backend, whose keys are signed strings containing {{{:}}}, {{{-}}}, {{{_}}} and uppercase letters.

This was first reported to security@djangoproject.com, and the security team asked for a public ticket.

I prepared this report and patch with help from Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic) via Claude Code, and I reviewed and verified the output myself.

ticket_data.title: Run async signal receivers sequentially
ticket_data.description:
Since async signal support was added, `Signal.send()` and `Signal.asend()` run async receivers concurrently. This causes two problems:

 * '''Registration order is lost.''' In sync Django, receivers run in the order they were registered, and projects often rely on this for good reasons. With async receivers, the order is lost silently, so converting a receiver from sync to async can change behavior.
 * '''Transactions inside receivers are not well ordered.''' Since each receiver runs in its own task, their queries and savepoints can interleave. This came up in the review of async `transaction.atomic()` (#33882, [https://github.com/django/django/pull/22074 PR #22074]): receivers can't use `atomic()` inside an async transaction, and inside a sync transaction a write from one receiver can be silently rolled back with another receiver's savepoint.

'''Proposal:''' await async receivers one by one, in registration order, in the caller's task. This keeps the same semantics as sync receivers and makes transaction handling inside receivers safe.

'''Trade-off:''' slow receivers would no longer run concurrently. This is a behavior change and would need a release note.

ticket_data.title: FieldError for annotation excluded by previous values() call incorrectly refers to unpromoted alias
ticket_data.description:
#36352 improved the `FieldError` message text when an annotation alias is requested via `values()` after being excluded by an earlier `values()` call.

However, it doesn't handle the case where the prior values call excludes ''all'' annotations, as in the last example below:

[https://dryorm.xterm.info/bugfield-error-message DryORM fiddle]
{{{#!py
from django.db import models

ticket_data.title: Test client responses form a reference cycle via `response.json` and need a GC pass to be freed
ticket_data.description:
`Client.request()` and `AsyncClient.request()` attach a `json` helper to every response as {{{#!python response.json = partial(self._parse_json, response) }}} ([https://github.com/django/django/blob/main/django/test/client.py#L1132 client.py#L1132], [https://github.com/django/django/blob/main/django/test/client.py#L1524 #L1524]). The `partial` holds a strong reference to the response and is stored on the response itself, so every response returned by the test client is part of a reference cycle. Reference counting can never free it; it survives until the cyclic garbage collector runs. Because the response also holds `response.templates`, `response.context` (every `Context`/`RequestContext` rendered during the request), `response.request`, `response.wsgi_request` and the rendered content, the whole graph stays alive with it. This is the same class of problem as #36701 (`ModelState` cycles), which was accepted and fixed. === Impact === On a large suite (~11k tests, many of them making admin requests) this was the main source of cyclic garbage. With Python 3.14.0–3.14.4 (incremental GC, reverted in 3.14.5) the garbage was collected much more slowly than it was produced: a single pytest-xdist worker grew from ~360 MB to ~1.8 GB over 1266 tests, and `-n auto` on a 14-core / 14 GB machine exhausted RAM. With the generational GC the garbage does get collected, but every test-client response still has to be reclaimed by a gen-2 pass instead of being freed on `del`, which means extra GC work and a higher memory peak in long suites. === Reproduction (standalone, no project needed) === {{{#!python import gc import django from django.conf import settings settings.configure( ROOT_URLCONF=__name__, ALLOWED_HOSTS=["testserver"], SECRET_KEY="x", TEMPLATES=[{"BACKEND": "django.template.backends.django.DjangoTemplates"}], ) django.setup() from django.http import HttpResponse from django.template import engines from django.test import Client from django.test.utils import setup_test_environment from django.urls import path def view(request): tpl = engines["django"].from_string("{% for i in r %}

{{ i }}

{% endfor %}") return HttpResponse(tpl.render({"r": range(50)})) urlpatterns = [path("", view)] setup_test_environment() c = Client() c.get("/") gc.disable() gc.collect() r = c.get("/") del r print("objects in cycles after one request:", gc.collect()) # 71 r = c.get("/") del r.json del r print("same, after removing response.json:", gc.collect()) # 0 }}} Output (Django 5.2.19 and main, Python 3.14.9; same on 3.14.4): {{{ objects in cycles after one request: 71 same, after removing response.json: 0 }}} `response.json` is the only cycle. Once it is removed, nothing is left for the collector. === Possible fix === Keep a weak reference to the response in the helper: {{{#!python response.json = partial(self._parse_json, weakref.proxy(response)) }}} (in both `Client.request()` and `AsyncClient.request()`). `response.json()` keeps working, and the parsed result is still cached on `response._json` (#27516). With this change the reproduction above reports `0` objects in cycles. The only behaviour change is that calling a detached `json` after the response itself has been released raises `ReferenceError`, e.g. `f = client.get(...).json; f()`. That seems unlikely in practice. If it matters, `json` could instead be exposed through a small descriptor. A regression test could assert that, with `gc.disable()`, a response from `client.get()` is freed as soon as it is deleted. For example, take a `weakref.ref(response)`, then `del response`, and check that the ref is `None` without calling `gc.collect()`.

ticket_data.title: Python 3.16 compatibility.
ticket_data.description:
Python 3.16 final is scheduled for October 2027 (see ​​​[https://peps.python.org/pep-0826/ PEP 826]). This is a tracking ticket for compatibility fixes for Django submitted in the meantime.

Django 6.2 will be the first version to support Python 3.16, because Django 6.1 will end the mainstream support in April 2027.

ticket_data.title: Avoid importing ctypes at import time in django.core.files.locks on Windows
ticket_data.description:
On Windows, django/core/files/locks.py imports ctypes and ctypes.wintypes and defines the OVERLAPPED structure and the LockFileEx/UnlockFileEx prototypes at module level. The module is imported by django.core.cache.backends.filebased, which django.core.checks imports, so every `import django.db.models` on Windows imports ctypes and loads _ctypes.pyd, libffi and the OLE DLLs _ctypes links against, whether or not anything ever locks a file. On other platforms the module only imports fcntl.

Measured on Windows 11 with Python 3.14.4 and Django main (8e3dec6):

- `python -X importtime -c "import django.db.models"`: django.core.files.locks takes 11.2 ms cumulative on Windows (0.1 ms on Linux, same machine under WSL2).
- Building the ctypes objects on the first lock()/unlock() call instead: `import django.db.models` is 6.0 ms faster (310.7 -> 300.9 ms, 95% CI 1.2-13.6 ms, 60 alternating runs timed inside the process).

The constants and the lock/unlock functions stay at module level, so the public behavior is unchanged. `runtests.py files cache file_storage` passes on Windows with the change.

I'd be happy to submit the patch.

AI disclosure: the patch was prepared with GitHub Copilot (Claude Opus 5.5 model), which was used to find the import, and write the patch.

ticket_data.title: set_cookie() ignores the cookie flags required by name prefixes and SameSite=None
ticket_data.description:
`HttpResponse.set_cookie()` emits the `secure` and `httponly` values exactly as it receives them, while
`HttpResponse.delete_cookie()` already applies the flags a browser requires before it stores a cookie.
The result is a syntactically valid `Set-Cookie` header that the browser silently discards.

This affects three documented cases:

|| Cookie name / parameters || Required by the browser || Emitted by set_cookie() ||
|| `__Secure-x`, `__Host-x`, `__Http-x` || `Secure` || nothing, unless the caller passes `secure=True` ||
|| `__Http-x`, `__Host-Http-x` || `HttpOnly` || nothing, unless the caller passes `httponly=True` ||
|| `samesite="None"` || `Secure` || nothing ||

References: RFC 6265bis section 4.1.3 (cookie name prefixes) and the SameSite=None requirements. The
`__Http-` and `__Host-Http-` prefixes come from CHIPS; `delete_cookie()` already handles them, so the
inconsistency is inside the same class.

The failure is silent. The response is a normal 200 with a `Set-Cookie` header, the browser drops the
cookie, and the following request arrives without it. A project that sets
`SESSION_COOKIE_NAME = "__Host-sessionid"` and keeps `SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = False` (local development,
or TLS terminated in a reverse proxy) sees a successful login followed by a request with no session, and
nothing appears in the server logs.

Steps to reproduce, current behavior:

{{{
>>> from django.http import HttpResponse
>>> r = HttpResponse()
>>> r.set_cookie("__Host-sessionid", "abc")
>>> r.cookies["__Host-sessionid"]["secure"]
''
>>> r.set_cookie("c", "abc", samesite="None")
>>> r.cookies["c"]["secure"]
''
}}}

Expected behavior: `secure` is `True` in both cases, because a browser will not store either cookie
otherwise. Cookies without a name prefix and without `SameSite=None` must keep behaving exactly as
before, with the flags the caller passed and nothing else.

Proposed fix: a module-level helper in `django/http/response.py` that computes the flags required by the
name and by `samesite`, used by both `set_cookie()` and `delete_cookie()` so the two paths cannot
diverge again. The helper only adds flags a browser already requires for that cookie; it never removes
one.

Patch: https://github.com/django/django/pull/22261 (branch `set-cookie-required-flags`), with four
regression tests in `tests/responses/test_cookie.py` and a paragraph in
`docs/ref/request-response.txt`.

Verification:

{{{
$ python tests/runtests.py responses --parallel 1     # with the patch
Ran 61 tests
OK (skipped=1)

$ python tests/runtests.py responses --parallel 1     # django/http/response.py reverted
FAILED (failures=7, skipped=1)
}}}

The seven failures are exactly the new assertions (the prefixed-name loops count one subtest each), so
they measure the change and not the environment.

Not covered by this patch: `__Host-` also requires `Path=/` and no `Domain` attribute. Enforcing that
means changing the contract of `set_cookie()` or adding a `security.W0xx` deployment check that reads
`SESSION_COOKIE_NAME` / `CSRF_COOKIE_NAME`; it can be a follow-up rather than part of this diff.

I searched the existing tickets for cookie prefixes, `Secure`, `HttpOnly` and `SameSite`. The open ones I
found, including 34613 (`Partitioned` support) and the older cookie parsing tickets, do not cover
`set_cookie()` applying the flags required by name prefixes or by `SameSite=None`.
